title: Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris
author: Agnel Philip
content:
When SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket exploded over the Caribbean last year, the
internet lit up with videos from airline passengers, island tourists and
locals showing flaming debris shooting across the sky. Even some airline
pilots recorded the fiery aftermath as [planes scrambled to move out of its
path](https://www.propublica.org/article/spacex-faa-launch-airlines-safety-
explosions-florida-caribbean).

Some of those videos of Starship’s seventh test flight — including ones taken
from Disney and Royal Caribbean cruise ships and a Club Med resort — went on
to play a role in the company's efforts to count and track pieces of debris
after the explosion, a report obtained by ProPublica says.

The report — obtained by ProPublica from the Federal Aviation Administration
through a freedom of information request — shows video captured a fireball,
then a shower of sparkling debris in the sky moments after the explosion. It
includes maps pinpointing where the images were shot, which helped the company
understand how debris tumbled to earth after the blast.

“At 1 minute 42 seconds, the debris cloud is observed transiting behind the
cruise ship,” says the report, which SpaceX provided the FAA two weeks after
the so-called mishap.

Such reports are required by federal rules in the days after a rocket failure
and are supposed to describe what happened and where hazardous debris landed.
The information is key for the FAA’s efforts to keep busy air traffic
corridors safe at a time of rapid growth in the commercial space industry as
companies like SpaceX develop and test rockets that they hope will eventually
reach the moon and Mars.

During launches, the FAA preventively closes airspace. It has also been forced
to clear areas quickly after test flights of massive spacecraft went wrong.

Starship flights 7 and 8 broke apart last year and scattered debris above
airline traffic over the Caribbean. Before Flight 9, the FAA moved to greatly
increase the size of the airspace it walled off pre-launch.

The agency defined its no-fly zones, which are closed to airplane traffic
during a launch, and its so-called debris response areas, which are closed
after a mishap, using information from SpaceX and modeling from Space Force,
the branch of the military that deals with the nation’s space interests, to
predict where debris might fall.

Nearly doubling those pre-launch no-fly zones “only makes sense if the prior
margin was judged inadequate rather than just unlucky,” said Moriba Jah, a
professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Austin.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/122225-spacex-
promo-final.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **“We’re Too Close to the Debris”**
](https://www.propublica.org/article/spacex-faa-launch-airlines-safety-
explosions-florida-caribbean)

Earlier this year, [the FAA issued a
warning](https://www.propublica.org/article/faa-safety-warning-spacex-
starship-explosions-airlines) that rocket launches could “significantly reduce
safety” for airplanes, after [ProPublica reported that 21
planes](https://www.propublica.org/article/spacex-faa-launch-airlines-safety-
explosions-florida-caribbean) appeared to make sudden turns to exit or avoid
an FAA-designated emergency no-fly zone in the minutes after the Flight 7
explosion. Such disruptions are likely to become more frequent. SpaceX is
seeking to launch Starship up to 76 times a year from Cape Canaveral, Florida.

The FAA provided ProPublica the reports on Starship flights 7, 8 and 9 — all
of which involved mishaps — after we requested them under the Freedom of
Information Act. The FAA redacted the vast majority of all three reports,
citing, among other things, exemptions in the law that protect confidential
business information from disclosure. The blackouts were, in part, a
reflection of SpaceX’s objections; FAA allowed the company to challenge the
release of information it deemed proprietary.

The FAA refused to release information that would show SpaceX’s estimates of
where debris fell during the three rocket failures. It’s unclear what the
agency or the company knows about how close any airplanes came to falling
debris.

“Withholding the underlying debris estimates makes it impossible for anyone
outside SpaceX and FAA to check whether that pattern is improving or
repeating,” Jah said. “Given a regulator already revised its own safety
margins once, the public has a real interest in seeing the data behind both
the old margin and the new one.”

The unredacted part of the report did not show whether the debris from the
Flight 7 explosion fell where SpaceX and the FAA expected it to. But the
references to Disney and Club Med guests’ video suggest SpaceX did not have a
full picture of where the debris landed without them. “I would read it as
evidence their own tracking did not carry cleanly through the debris cloud
phase, so they used the public to fill the gap,” Jah said.

![A document with two maps and four screenshots of videos. Two of the
screenshots show an explosion in the sky. One of the screenshots shows an
illuminated water slide.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/crop_REDACTED_-Starship_Flight_7_450.103d_Report-AST-
Redactions_Redacted-2-27_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg)A page from SpaceX’s
report shows the company used public video, including from near a Disney
cruise ship, to track debris from Starship Flight 7. Obtained by ProPublica.
Redactions in original document.

SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The company has said that it
learns from its mistakes and that each test improves Starship’s reliability.
Last December, it said on X that “SpaceX is committed to responsibly using
airspace during launches and reentries, prioritizing public safety to protect
people on the ground, at sea, and in the air.”

The FAA did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Disney, Royal
Caribbean or Club Med.

Ron Madler, a professor of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical
University, said the videos could help SpaceX “either confirm their breakup
models or possibly to improve them.”

The mishap report for Flight 8, which rained debris near the Bahamas, said
before that flight’s explosive failure, SpaceX did not have the proper “test
stand” that was capable of testing the rocket’s engines “for a full Starship
mission.” The remainder of the page was blacked out, so it was unclear from
the report whether the company had found another way to fully test the engines
before launch.

Flights 7 and 8 both involved the same model. Both ended in engine-related
failures.

Text in the report around the statement about the test stand was redacted. But
Jah said it “means some part of the engine’s actual flight behavior was being
verified for the first time in flight rather than on the ground.”

John Crassidis, an aerospace engineering professor at the University at
Buffalo, said launching before having a fully capable test stand was likely “a
cost-saving decision.” In building rockets, he said, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has
used both the old approach of launching and then fixing any issues that arise,
and the newer approach of running simulations and ground tests first to head
off problems.

“Doing too much of the old school can lead to too many mishaps and cost
overruns,” he said. “Doing too much of the new school leads to long times to
get things done and a reduction in flexibility.”

The post [Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used
Bystander Videos to Track Falling
Debris](https://www.propublica.org/article/spacex-starship-caribbean-
explosion-report) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
